comparisons.title: Points over expected vs true shooting percentage
comparisons.question: What is the difference between points over expected and true shooting percentage?
comparisons.lead: True shooting percentage asks how efficiently a player scored. Points over expected asks how much he scored above what his shots were worth. The first is an efficiency rate, the second is a residual against a model, and they disagree whenever a player's shot diet is unusually easy or unusually hard.

theirs.name: True shooting percentage
theirs.what: Points per scoring attempt, counting free throws at a fixed 0.44 weight.

rows: Yes, every attempt is priced by location and context
No, a layup and a stepback count the same
Yes, above the rate the situation usually produces
Yes, but at a fixed 0.44 weight per attempt
None; it is an absolute rate
comparisons.use: Use true shooting to ask who scored efficiently. Use points over expected to ask who beat the shots they took. A high-TS% rim finisher and a high-POE pull-up shooter are doing different things.
comparisons.neither: Neither separates a player from his team's spacing or playmaking, and neither measures defence.

comparisons.title: Points over expected vs effective field goal percentage
comparisons.question: How does points over expected differ from effective field goal percentage?
comparisons.lead: Effective field goal percentage credits a three as worth 1.5 twos and stops there. Points over expected goes further: it prices every attempt by how likely it was to go in from where and how it was taken, then reports the gap.

theirs.name: Effective field goal percentage
theirs.what: Field goal percentage with threes weighted for their extra point.

rows: Separately: shot value and shot-making are different lenses
comparisons.use: Effective field goal percentage is the better quick read on shooting mix. Points over expected is the better read on whether a player exceeded his own looks.
comparisons.neither: Neither can see how open the shooter was; openness is not in the public data.

comparisons.title: Shot quality vs shot-making
comparisons.question: What is the difference between shot quality and shot-making?
comparisons.lead: They are the two halves this site deliberately keeps apart. Shot quality is what the looks were worth before anyone shot them. Shot-making is whether the player beat those looks. A player can be excellent at one and poor at the other.
rows: Lower: shooting varies year to year
comparisons.use: Read them together. A rising shot-value figure driven by shot quality is a different claim from one driven by shot-making, and only the first is mostly under a team's control.
comparisons.neither: Neither attributes shot quality between the player, the system and the coach.

comparisons.title: RAPM vs box plus/minus
comparisons.question: Is RAPM better than box plus/minus?
comparisons.lead: Box plus/minus estimates impact from box-score production. RAPM estimates it from what happened while a player was on the floor, holding teammates and opponents fixed. They are answering the same question from different evidence, and RAPM's evidence is closer to the question.

theirs.name: Box plus/minus
theirs.what: A regression that predicts a player's impact per 100 possessions from his box-score line and his team's performance.

rows: Sees things the box score misses
High; shrunk toward a box-score prior
Low, because the box score is stable
comparisons.use: This site uses RAPM, and uses a box-score prior to shrink it where possessions are thin, which is an attempt to take the strengths of both. On a full season of possessions prefer RAPM; on a few hundred prefer the prior.
comparisons.neither: Neither is causal, and neither can separate a player from the lineups he happened to play in.

comparisons.title: EuroLeague vs NBA shot difficulty
comparisons.question: Are EuroLeague shots harder than NBA shots?
comparisons.lead: This site cannot answer that, and the reason is worth stating rather than hiding. The expected-points model is fit **separately for each league** and anchored to each season's own league rate, so a figure means "against this league, this season" and nothing more. Comparing the raw numbers across leagues compares two different yardsticks.
comparisons.tableNote: Current season per league. Shown because the figures are real and often asked for, NOT because they are comparable: each column comes from a model fit on that league alone.
comparisons.use: Use them within a league. To compare leagues you would need one model fit across all of them on a shared feature set, which the differing public feeds do not currently support.
comparisons.neither: No number here supports a claim that one league's shots are harder than another's.

comparisons.title: Expected points vs expected value
comparisons.question: What is the difference between expected points and expected value in basketball?
comparisons.lead: Expected points values a shot that was taken. Expected value, as this site uses it in the clutch-decision layer, values a choice between options at the moment it was made, in win probability rather than points.
rows: No, and a test asserts it
comparisons.use: Expected points tells you whether a shot was a good shot. Expected value tells you whether it was the right shot to take in that situation.
comparisons.neither: Neither says whether the shot went in, which is the point of both.

comparisons.title: Free throws over expected vs free throw rate
comparisons.question: How is free throws over expected different from free throw rate?
comparisons.lead: Free throw rate counts trips to the line per shot. Free throws over expected asks whether a player draws more than his situations usually produce, which separates a player who seeks contact from one who simply shoots a lot of layups.
rows: Only above what the rim usually draws
comparisons.use: Free throw rate is the simpler description. Free throws over expected is the one that isolates the part not explained by where a player shoots.
comparisons.neither: Neither distinguishes contact-seeking skill from the officiating a player happens to receive.

comparisons.title: Defensive rating vs shot quality forced
comparisons.question: Is defensive rating or shot quality forced the better measure of a defence?
comparisons.lead: Defensive rating counts what a defence conceded. Shot quality forced prices what it allowed opponents to attempt, before those attempts went in or out. The second is far more repeatable, which the site measured rather than assumed.

theirs.name: Defensive rating
theirs.what: Points a team concedes per 100 defensive possessions.

rows: Separates shot quality from opponent shooting
Split-half reliability on this site's data
Expected points per shot vs league
comparisons.use: Use shot quality forced to ask what a defence makes opponents do, and points allowed as the unadjusted outcome. The site publishes both and orders its defensive pillars by measured reliability.
comparisons.neither: Neither is a player metric. The shot-level player version was built and rejected at 0.348 split-half reliability.
